section: Informal Definition; Non-Zero Natural Numbers; Peano's Axioms
context: Elementary arithmetic: N contains 0; N_{>0} used when zero must be excluded
definition: In the convention used here, the natural numbers are the elements of N={0,1,2,3,…}. The strictly positive natural numbers form N_{>0}=N\{0}={1,2,3,…}.
review: ProofWiki explicitly records both zero-including and zero-excluding conventions, then a separate Peano axiomatization. For integer construction, N includes 0 so [a,b] may model negative, zero and positive differences; no claim is made that a concrete set of von Neumann ordinals is literally identical to every Peano model. The Peano axioms are an alternative axiomatic characterization, not interchangeable set-theoretic underlying objects.
alt_variants_to_consider: Peano system (N,0,s); von Neumann finite ordinals; positive-index convention

context: Set theory: binary relation on a set with reflexivity, symmetry and transitivity
definition: An equivalence relation ∼ on a set S is a subset R⊆S×S such that x∼x for every x∈S; x∼y implies y∼x; and x∼y together with y∼z implies x∼z for all x,y,z∈S.
review: ProofWiki Definition 1 gives the three exact conditions. The Stacks Project similarly treats relations on a set as subsets of S×S and equivalence as reflexive symmetric transitive; geometric equivalence relations of schemes are a distinct context and must not replace this one. The integer pairs construction uses an equivalence relation on N×N, which is mathematically separate from the sequence-equivalence relation used to construct real numbers.
alt_variants_to_consider: Diagonal/inverse/composition relation inclusion characterization; categorical equivalence relation

context: Set-theoretic class of elements related to a chosen representative
definition: Given an equivalence relation ∼ on S and x∈S, the equivalence class of x is [x]={y∈S:y∼x}. Each element of [x] is a representative of that class.
review: Source defines the class as the subset of S containing all elements equivalent to x and identifies representatives. Since ∼ is symmetric, {y:y∼x} and {y:x∼y} are equal. The class is a subset of S, not the singleton {x} unless all equivalence classes are singletons. This class precedes the quotient S/∼ and provides the element construction for integers.

context: Set of equivalence classes under a fixed equivalence relation
definition: For an equivalence relation ∼ on a set S, the quotient set S/∼ is the set of all its equivalence classes: S/∼={[x]:x∈S}. Its elements are equivalence classes, not individual elements of S.
review: ProofWiki defines the quotient precisely as the set of equivalence classes under a specified relation. The canonical quotient map x↦[x] is a separately defined function and the universal factorization property is a theorem, not an additional quotient-set definition. Care is required not to confuse the underlying quotient set with a quotient ring/group which requires compatible operations.
alt_variants_to_consider: Quotient defined via a partition into nonempty disjoint classes, with partition/equivalence correspondence proven separately
